slides.title: Section 5 · Application — In Practice
slides.notes:
SECTION 5 · APPLICATION — IN PRACTICE
The Cross-CXO Organisational Health Clinic: From Functional Health Assessments to Enterprise People-Performance Restoration

HOW THIS SECTION RUNS:
Nine parts in order: 5.1 Application Overview; 5.2 Functional Organisational Health Assessment (Task 1); 5.3 Quantifying Functional People-Performance Losses (Task 2); 5.4 Consolidating the Capstone Group Health Position (Tasks 3 and 4); 5.5 Quantifying Losses Across the Selected Functions (Tasks 5 and 6); 5.6 Review–Realign–Restore; 5.7 Consolidated Organisational Health Response (Task 7); 5.8 Build Your Cultural Operating Code (Task 8); 5.9 Capstone Assessment Output. This is group Capstone work: each group completes one shared record, which goes into boxes 11A to 11E of its Capstone S2R® Blueprint.

SECTION LEARNING OUTCOMES:
1. Consolidate functional organisational health assessments and quantify enterprise-level people-performance losses to establish an evidence-based organisational health position.
2. Commit the executive team to coordinated remedial actions and shared behavioural norms that restore people performance and strengthen organisational health.

HOW TO OPEN THE SECTION:

1. Frame the Clinic.
Say: "Section 4 gave you the Cross-CXO Health Architecture. In this Clinic you use it as an executive team: you bring the functional positions together for collective executive decision-making."

2. Read the outcomes.
Read both section learning outcomes aloud.

3. Bridge to 5.1.
Say: "Here is what your group will do."

slides.title: 5.1 · The Clinic: four pieces of group work
slides.notes:
5.1 — APPLICATION OVERVIEW

HOW TO TEACH IT:

1. Recap what the Clinic builds on.
Say: "Individual employees independently complete the Organisational Health Thermometer; their responses are consolidated into functional health scores. Each CXO interprets the consolidated results, investigates potential cultural vulnerabilities and estimates associated people-performance losses. This capstone application brings the functional positions together for collective executive decision-making."

2. Walk the four pieces of work.
Say: "Your group uses only the CXO roles already assigned within your capstone group. You will, one, interpret the corresponding functional assessments; two, consolidate the scores and losses for those represented functions; three, determine remedial actions through Review–Realign–Restore; and four, build the organisation's Cultural Operating Code from its values."

3. Give the capstone instruction.
Say: "Each of you assesses the function associated with your existing capstone CXO role. Your group consolidates only the functions represented by its members. The 10 functional examples are a reference set from which your group selects its relevant roles; there is no requirement to assess or include all 10 functions. The completed group analysis is used in the final capstone panel assessment."

4. Bridge to Tasks 1 and 2.
Say: "The work starts with each function."

LATER, WHEN THE GROUPS DO THE WORK ON THE PORTAL:
Each group chooses its scribe for this work in the group record bar. The scribe types what the group agrees, and the entries appear on every member's page. In part 5.2 the group ticks the CXO roles represented in the group; roles named in the Problem Charter's executive team are ticked already, and the scribe can change them. When the record is complete, each member selects Agree, and the group's work goes into boxes 11A to 11E of the team's Capstone S2R® Blueprint.

slides.title: 5.2–5.3 · Tasks 1 and 2: each function
slides.notes:
5.2–5.3 — TASKS 1 AND 2: FUNCTIONAL HEALTH AND FUNCTIONAL LOSSES

HOW TO TEACH IT:

1. Explain the reference scores.
Say: "Part 5.2 gives example functional health scores consolidated from individual employee assessments using the Section 4 thermometer, for ten CXO functions: CEO 82, CFO 70, COO 50, CHRO 80, CTO/CIO 59, CMO 70, CCO 58, CPO 58, CRO 78 and CSO 66. Use only the rows corresponding to the CXO roles represented in your capstone group. Each trait is scored out of 20; the functional total is out of 100. Politics and Confusion refer to Minimal Politics and Minimal Confusion."

2. Teach Task 1.
Point to the left column.
Say: "Task 1, interpret the functional health position. Each of you uses your capstone CXO role and the thermometer to interpret the corresponding functional score. Determine the health classification, the two weakest traits, possible people-performance implications and evidence requiring further investigation."
Say: "The classifications: 80 to 100 Healthy & Thriving; 60 to 79 Stable but Uneven; 40 to 59 Caution Zone; 20 to 39 Unhealthy."
Say: "For each function you record: the CXO role and function, the functional score and classification, the two weakest traits, potential cultural vulnerabilities, and evidence requiring investigation."

3. Teach Task 2.
Point to the right column.
Say: "Part 5.3 gives illustrative preliminary gross quarterly exposure estimates in South African rand for each function, under the five hidden costs from Section 2. For example, the COO line totals R555,000 and the CEO line R28,000. Each estimate requires verification before it is treated as a financial loss."
Say: "Task 2, interpret functional losses. For the assigned function, identify the largest hidden cost, examine possible links to the two weakest health traits, specify evidence needed to validate the estimates, and flag any potential overlap or double counting. Distinguish estimated exposure from validated loss."

4. Bridge to the group position.
Say: "Once each function is read, the group consolidates."

LATER, WHEN THE GROUPS DO THE WORK ON THE PORTAL:
Each function the group ticked has its own card in part 5.2, for Task 1 and for Task 2. Guide the groups to complete one card per represented role, with the member who holds that role leading the entry.

slides.title: 5.4–5.5 · Tasks 3 to 6: the group position
slides.notes:
5.4–5.5 — TASKS 3 TO 6: THE GROUP HEALTH POSITION AND EXPOSURE

HOW TO TEACH IT:

1. Teach the weighted consolidation.
Point to the left column.
Say: "Consolidate only the functional assessments corresponding to the CXO roles represented in your capstone group. Weight each trait score by valid employee responses for those selected functions. The resulting consolidated position represents only the functions in the group."
Say: "Group Consolidated Trait Score equals the sum of each selected functional trait score times its valid responses, divided by the total valid responses in the selected functions. Group Consolidated Health Score equals the sum of the five weighted trait scores. This is the method you saw in 4.5."

2. Teach Tasks 3 and 4.
Say: "Task 3: calculate the consolidated score for each of the five traits and the consolidated health score out of 100."
Say: "Task 4: determine the consolidated score and thermometer classification for the functions represented in your group; identify the two weakest traits, the functions contributing most to those weaknesses, and the vulnerabilities requiring cross-functional leadership attention. Apply the result only to the functions assessed."

3. Teach Tasks 5 and 6.
Point to the right column.
Say: "Task 5: sum the functional estimates only for the CXO roles represented in your group, by hidden-cost category. Flag possible overlaps before presenting gross exposure as validated financial loss. Losses for unrepresented functions stay out of the total."
Say: "Task 6: establish the consolidated health diagnosis. Identify the two largest cost categories, the functions contributing most to gross exposure, plausible relationships between health traits and losses, and estimates requiring verification. A health score indicates where to look; financial causation requires evidence."
Say: "The diagnosis records the enterprise health score and classification, the two weakest traits, the most vulnerable functions, the gross quarterly exposure, the two largest hidden-cost categories, the priority cultural vulnerabilities and the priority people-performance concerns."

4. Bridge to 5.6.
Say: "With the position established, the executive team decides what to do about it."

LATER, WHEN THE GROUPS DO THE WORK ON THE PORTAL:
The page calculates the consolidated trait scores, the health score and the exposure from the roles the group ticked. The group writes its interpretation: the functions contributing most, the vulnerabilities requiring cross-functional attention, the overlaps flagged, and the diagnosis.

slides.title: 5.6 · Review–Realign–Restore
slides.notes:
5.6 — DETERMINE REMEDIAL ACTIONS THROUGH REVIEW–REALIGN–RESTORE

HOW TO TEACH IT:

1. Connect to the cycle the programme has used.
Say: "You have used Review–Realign–Restore in Module 3 for performance. Here it is applied to organisational health."

2. Review.
Say: "Review: establish priority health concerns. Examine the consolidated health position, functional vulnerabilities and financial exposure. Determine which traits require attention, which functions are affected, what employee experiences may explain the scores, and what supporting evidence is available. Output: a prioritised organisational health diagnosis."
Deepen, say: "The surface complaint is often the one that is safe to raise. The real issue, about authority, recognition or influence, is harder to name."
(Insight: Stated issue and real issue. Source: Journal, 6 March 2026 — Professional Insights)

3. Realign.
Say: "Realign: reinforce cultural conditions. Identify the organisational values, behavioural expectations and leadership practices requiring reinforcement. Determine the cross-functional expectations and CXO accountabilities needed to address the diagnosed conditions. Output: agreed cultural reinforcement actions with named executive accountability."

4. Restore.
Say: "Restore: establish measurable improvement. Set next-quarter improvement expectations for priority health traits and associated financial exposures. Define the evidence and review measures that will show whether employee experiences and people-performance conditions are improving. Output: measurable health and performance commitments."
Deepen, say: "Organisations that discover a fundamental misalignment between stated values and actual practice face a choice: respond completely, or address only what is comfortable. The part left untouched is the part that resurfaces."
(Insight: A complete response. Source: Journal, 29 June 2026 — Professional Insights: Strategy)

5. Bridge to 5.7.
Say: "The three outputs come together in one response."

LATER, WHEN THE GROUPS DO THE WORK ON THE PORTAL:
The group records one output for each step: the prioritised diagnosis, the reinforcement actions with named executive accountability, and the measurable commitments.

slides.title: 5.7 · Task 7: the Organisational Health Response
slides.notes:
5.7 — TASK 7: THE CONSOLIDATED ORGANISATIONAL HEALTH RESPONSE

HOW TO TEACH IT:

1. Explain the task.
Say: "Identify the lowest-scoring health trait from the consolidated assessment of the CXO functions represented in your capstone group. Apply Review–Realign–Restore to agree on the remedial action, assign the accountable CXO or CXOs, set a health improvement target, identify the associated hidden cost and establish a financial reduction target."

2. Walk the columns.
Say: "The response has six columns: the priority health trait; the Review–Realign–Restore action; the accountable CXO or CXOs; the health improvement target; the associated hidden cost; and the financial target, written as current, target and reduction."

3. Set the discipline.
Say: "Use one row for the lowest-scoring health trait. Add another row only if your group identifies a further priority requiring a distinct response. Financial targets are illustrative commitments and should be supported by evidence; avoid double counting."
Deepen, say: "Reorganisations, communications drives and new frameworks can multiply as substitutes for the one hard conversation that is actually required. Name it and schedule it."
(Insight: The avoided conversation. Source: Journal, 11 May 2026 — Professional Insights: Leadership)

4. Bridge to 5.8.
Say: "The response sets out what must change. Your Cultural Operating Code defines the behaviours that carry the change."

LATER, WHEN THE GROUPS DO THE WORK ON THE PORTAL:
The group completes one row of the response for its lowest-scoring trait, and a second row only for a further distinct priority.

slides.title: 5.8 · Task 8: build your Cultural Operating Code
slides.notes:
5.8 — TASK 8: BUILD YOUR CULTURAL OPERATING CODE

HOW TO TEACH IT:

1. Link the Code to the response.
Say: "Your Organisational Health Response sets out what must change. Your Cultural Operating Code defines the behaviours that carry the change: it translates your organisation's values into norms your executive team models, recognises and corrects. You build it the way part 4.7 showed with the IBSL Code."

2. Step 1: your organisation's values.
Say: "List the values of your capstone organisation, three to six, each with what it means in one line. Where your organisation's values are not yet stated, agree them now as its executive team."
Deepen, say: "Value clarity must come before commercial pressure."
(Insight: Values before commercial pressure. Source: Journal, 16 January 2026 — Professional Insights: Culture)

3. Step 2: translate the values into norms.
Say: "Translate at least three of your values. For each: the value, the observable behaviour, the acronym from three action words, the three actions and the norm statement. Begin each norm with the behaviour; the acronym only packages it."

4. Step 3: test your strongest norm.
Say: "Choose your strongest norm and record how it passes each of the three tests from part 4.7, the New Employee Test, the Pressure Test and the Mirror Test, or what your group changed so that it passes."

5. Say where it goes.
Say: "Your Cultural Operating Code forms part of the final capstone panel assessment, in Capstone box 11E."

6. Bridge to 5.9.
Say: "Here is what the panel will see from this unit."

LATER, WHEN THE GROUPS DO THE WORK ON THE PORTAL:
Each group builds the Code for its capstone organisation, using that organisation's values. Where a group has not yet stated its organisation's values, it agrees them first as the executive team. Guide the groups to begin each norm with the behaviour and to apply the three tests from part 4.7 to their strongest norm before they agree the record.

slides.title: 5.9 · Capstone assessment output
slides.notes:
5.9 — CAPSTONE ASSESSMENT OUTPUT

HOW TO TEACH IT:

1. Describe the output.
Say: "The completed Organisational Health Response forms part of the final capstone panel assessment. It includes the consolidated health score and gross quarterly exposure for only the functions represented in your group, the lowest-scoring health trait and one integrated Review–Realign–Restore response with accountable CXO or CXOs, a health improvement target and a financial reduction target. It also includes your group's Cultural Operating Code."

2. Walk the five Capstone boxes.
Say: "11A, Functional health assessments: for each CXO function represented in your executive team, the functional health score and classification and the two weakest traits, with your interpretation."
Say: "11B, Consolidated health position: the response-weighted health score and classification for the represented functions, the weakest traits and the gross quarterly exposure."
Say: "11C, Review–Realign–Restore: the prioritised organisational health diagnosis, the cultural reinforcement actions with named executive accountability, and the measurable commitments."
Say: "11D, Organisational Health Response: for the lowest-scoring health trait, the action, accountable CXO or CXOs, health improvement target, associated hidden cost and financial target."
Say: "11E, Cultural Operating Code: your organisation's values, each translated norm, and your strongest norm with how it passes the three tests."

3. Set the presentation expectation.
Say: "This work is presented only during the final capstone panel assessment."

4. Bridge to the close.
Say: "Let us close the unit."
Point the groups to their company overview. Say: "Your company overview, just above the group record bar, shows your company, your trigger, your three problems and your central problem statement. Every part of this work is done for that company and its central problem."

slides.title: Closing · Transition to Unit 12

CLOSING · TRANSITION TO UNIT 12

HOW TO TEACH IT:

1. Give the Section 5 Closing Insight.
Say: "Organisational health improves when the executive team reads it from evidence, prices what poor health costs, acts on the lowest-scoring conditions with named accountability, and models the norms of its Cultural Operating Code."

2. Return to the progression of the unit.
Say: "We began with one progression. Values establish behavioural principles. Culture reflects how these principles are lived. Organisational health reflects the resulting collective condition. You have now read that condition, priced it and set out the norms that will change it."
Ask: "Which one norm from your group's Code will be hardest for you, personally, to model next quarter?"
Listen for: honest answers that name a behaviour; connect them to the Mirror Test.

3. Bridge to Unit 12.
